newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch hand on Euro-presidency after modest advance.
newsitem.headline: Dutch hand on Euro-presidency after modest advance.

text.p: The Netherlands will pass the European Union presidency baton to Luxembourg next week with a new EU treaty criticised by many as more of a face-saving exercise than a real step forward.
Billed beforehand as the pact to take the 15-nation bloc into the next millennium, the revised treaty brokered in Amsterdam earlier this month leaves a number of loose ends waiting to be tied up.

Planned reforms to streamline EU institutions in preparation for the inclusion of the bloc's former communist eastern neighbours have mostly been put on ice, while Britain and Ireland again secured opt-outs from measures aimed at harmonising policy across the member states.

The summit's one triumph -- a compromise on a budgetary stability pact incorporating a resolution on boosting employment -- is largely a fudge whose substantive elements were prepared under Ireland's EU presidency, according to one academic expert.

"If you look at the outcome of the Dutch EU presidency and the Amsterdam summit, nothing substantial has really been achieved -- it's all window dressing, including the jobs chapter," says Dr Otto Holman, specialist in European affairs at the University of Amsterdam.
Set against the substantive achievements laid down in the Maastricht treaty under the previous Dutch EU presidency six years ago, Amsterdam just does not compare, Holman argues.
"Then, European member states laid down the framework for monetary union; now they have made only limited progress on decision-making procedures," he says.
Members of the European Parliament meeting in Brussels took the same view on Thursday, slamming the lack of progress in introducing qualified majority voting across a broad range of policy areas.
Briefing the parliament on the Netherlands presidency and the summit, Dutch premier Wim Kok had to concede he, too, had hoped for more.
Nevertheless he insisted the Amsterdam Treaty did represent a real step forward.

"Despite all the concessions we had to make, (this) is a treaty which has definitely been worth the trouble," he said. "(It heralds) a Europe of the citizen that is more democratic and more transparent."
Other member states have been even less enthusiastic about the modest gains booked at the Amsterdam summit while acknowledging the hurdles that had to be overcome.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told reporters back home that the summit had not failed to live up to expectations because Rome knew the European situation, but that it was "certainly below our hopes".
While European deputies and national politicians have expressed disappointment at the limited scope of treaty reforms, they have lauded the Dutch efforts to bring member states into line.
"Generally speaking foreign countries have been full of praise for the Dutch effort -- barring some isolated critique from Spain," notes Holman.
"All in all the Dutch are perceived to have handled the presidency very well because they did all they possibly could to make a success of things."
